analysis.one_liner: Doubles fines on hospitals that don't post their standard prices and publicly names violators.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing, a cosponsor, or any action since it was referred there in February 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal rules since 2021 require hospitals to publish the standard prices they charge for services, but the maximum fines are small and enforcement has been weak. This bill roughly doubles the maximum daily penalties for hospitals that don't comply (from $300 to $600 per day for small hospitals, from $10 to $20 per bed for mid-size ones, and from $5,500 to $11,000 for the largest) and orders Medicare's agency to publish, every six months, a list naming each hospital out of compliance. It also bars hospitals from hiding their price pages from online search results. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and employers, who could actually see hospital prices before getting care and compare them. Insurers and employers negotiating with hospitals also gain leverage from posted rates. The bill gives no new benefit checks; it strengthens an existing disclosure rule.

how_it_helps.text: Roughly doubles the maximum civil monetary penalties for hospitals that fail to publish and update their standard charge lists: $600/day for hospitals with 30 or fewer beds, $20 per bed/day for hospitals with 31 to 550 beds, and $11,000/day for hospitals with more than 550 beds.

Requires the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to publish a public list naming each hospital not in compliance with the price transparency requirements, beginning 280 days after enactment and every 180 days after.

Prohibits hospitals from shielding the required price information from online search results through webpage coding, and sets timing rules so every hospital operating in the U.S. must publish its price list within 6 months and update it annually.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which face larger fines, public naming if they don't post prices, and new compliance work. Patients would not pay the fines directly, though hospitals could argue higher compliance costs feed into prices.

drawbacks.text: Even the doubled maximums are small relative to hospital revenues, so the penalty ceiling may still not deter large hospital systems that price opacity is worth more to than an $11,000-a-day maximum, which is why some enforcement advocates have called for much larger fines.

Publishing standard charges does not tell patients what they will actually owe: insurers negotiate different rates, and a hospital's posted standard price often differs from the negotiated or discounted amount a patient pays.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: doubling the fines and naming violators makes an under-enforced transparency rule more likely to be followed, at little cost to anyone except noncompliant hospitals. The main limitation is design, not cost: standard charges are not the negotiated prices patients actually pay, so even full compliance would not hand patients a final bill before care. The bill is a step toward price visibility, not a price cap or billing guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no action on it since February 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kennedy introduced the Hospital Transparency Compliance Enforcement Act in the Senate on February 25, 2025.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral is the last recorded action in the bill's history.
No senators have cosponsored the bill, and it has not received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the Senate.

The bill would amend the Public Health Service Act to roughly double maximum civil monetary penalties for hospitals that fail to publish standard charges and to require a periodic public list of noncompliant hospitals.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that keep their prices hidden are better off so far, because the stronger fines and public shaming list have not been enacted. Patients who want comparable hospital prices get nothing from a bill that has not moved.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to double hospital price transparency fines and require a public list of noncompliant hospitals.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill, holding no hearing or markup, since it was referred there in February 2025.

against.name: American Hospital Association and hospital industry
against.role: Hospitals subject to the transparency rule
against.what_they_did: Has generally pushed back on price transparency mandates and enforcement since the 2021 rule took effect.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split has actually been tested.

industries.note: The bill roughly doubles the maximum daily fines for hospitals that fail to post standard charges and forces Medicare's agency to publicly name noncompliant hospitals. Hospitals benefit financially when patients cannot comparison-shop, so their interest in weaker enforcement runs against patients who want to see prices.
Posted hospital prices give employers buying health coverage for workers better data to negotiate lower rates. Workers and employers gain together.
Insurers negotiating against posted hospital rates get added leverage, which can lower premiums and cost-sharing for their members.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in the Senate HELP Committee with zero cosponsors and no hearing for their first year rarely come to a floor vote. With no committee action on the horizon, the most likely path is that the bill expires at the end of this Congress unless a companion proposal is attached to a larger health package.
